name: Sunset stripes (1979)
description: Midway's first scheme, from its first flights in November 1979: a white upper body over bare metal, with three equal stripes along the window line under the windows, orange over red over yellow on a thin navy line. Over the engines the white ends in a rounded end and the stripes turn up around it, each widening into an upright band over the crown, orange, red and yellow, so they read as a sunset. Behind them the whole tail is navy: the aft body, fin, tail cone and nacelles. On the fin a big orange disc crossed by a navy chevron pointing forward. 'Midway' in navy bold upright letters above the forward windows. Gray wings.

sources.title: Douglas DC-9-15 N1065T Midway Als DCA 26.06.82 (CC BY 3.0, RuthAS)
sources.note: DC-9-15 N1065T at Washington National, right side, nearly side-on, 26 June 1982: the stripes' heights, where they turn up and the bands' widths, the title and the fin's disc measured on it (drawnOn DC91), scaled by its windows (27.9 px/m) and its engine inlet.

sources.title: McDonnell Douglas DC-9-15, Midway Airlines (GFDL 1.2, Jon Proctor)
sources.note: DC-9-15 N1065T, left side from ahead, December 1980: the title's size and place behind the door, the stripes' order and the disc (26.9 px/m by its windows).

sources.title: Midway Airlines Douglas DC-9-14 N1056T (CC BY-SA 4.0, Richard Vandervord)
sources.note: DC-9-14 N1056T at Phoenix, right side, 1 October 1979, just delivered: the closest view of the stripes (orange, red and yellow over a thin navy line, bare metal under it), the white's rounded end and the bands wrapping it, and the tail mark.

sources.title: McDonnell Douglas DC-9-15, Midway Airlines (GFDL 1.2, Jon Proctor)
sources.note: DC-9-15 N1060T, right side from ahead, 11 December 1982: still in this scheme, the latest dated photo of it found.

sources.title: Midway Airlines (1976–1991), Wikipedia
sources.note: History: service from 1 November 1979 with DC-9-10s, eight DC-9-30s from Ansett by early 1982, the Metrolink scheme from 1983.

notes: Measured 2026-11-26 for ghost flights on DC-9-15 N1065T (June 1982, right side) on shapes/DC91.json, checked on the same aircraft from the left (December 1980) and on N1056T (October 1979). The stripes are each about 0.23 m tall, the navy line about 0.08 m, the orange's top just under the windows. The white ends over the engine inlet (about 18.3 m from the nose) in a rounded end; the bands behind it are about 0.95, 0.8 and 0.95 m wide where they run up over the crown, so each stripe widens about fourfold as it turns up, with rounder corners outward. The rounding of each corner is read from the 1979 photo and is the least sure part. The navy covers everything aft of the yellow band, crown to belly; where the bare metal belly ends under it is hidden by the wing and engine in every photo found, so it's drawn ending straight down under the yellow band. The stripes run forward level to the nose. The disc's mark is our own simplified drawing. Colors vary a lot between the slides (the red reads from red-orange to brick, the orange from amber to tangerine); the navy is near black in shade. The scheme lasted until the Metrolink scheme of 1983: N1060T still wore it in December 1982. No openly licensed photo of a DC-9-30 in this scheme was found, though Midway had eight from early 1982, so the DC-9-30 is fitted.

DC93.note: Fitted, not measured: Midway's DC-9-30s came from Ansett by early 1982, before the Metrolink scheme, so they likely wore this, but no photo of one in it was found. The DC-9-10's stripes at the same heights, the white's end over the engine inlet as on the DC-9-10 (22.85 m), the title at the same distance behind the door and the same size.
